title: Berkshire 1983 letter: Owner-partner principles, economic Goodwill vs book value, and the cost of hyperactive markets
summary: Buffett restates Berkshire's manager-owner principles (partnership attitude, per-share intrinsic value, ignoring accounting optics, candor, no dilution). He explains economic Goodwill via See's Candies, contrasts book value with intrinsic value, and argues against stock splits and hyperactive trading.

principles.text: Treat shareholders as partners, and the company as a conduit through which they own the assets.
principles.quote: Although our form is corporate, our attitude is partnership.

principles.text: Judge performance by per-share gains in intrinsic business value, not by size.
principles.quote: We do not measure the economic significance or performance of Berkshire by its size; we measure by per-share progress.

principles.text: Accounting optics should never drive capital allocation; prefer more unreported earnings over fewer reported ones.
principles.quote: Accounting consequences do not influence our operating or capital-allocation decisions.

principles.text: Book value records what has been put in; intrinsic value estimates discounted future cash that can be taken out.
principles.quote: Book value tells you what has been put in; intrinsic business value estimates what can be taken out.

principles.text: Franchise businesses needing few tangible assets are hurt least by inflation and create enduring economic Goodwill.
principles.quote: During inflation, Goodwill is the gift that keeps giving.

principles.text: A great business is not automatically a good purchase; price paid determines the return.
principles.quote: A good business is not always a good purchase – although it’s a good place to look for one.
